prompt: A component with a 6 ms service time runs at 80% of its 400/s capacity at peak. You move it to a size with 3 times the capacity and the same service time. What is its p99 now, to the nearest millisecond?

options.whyWrong: This is p99 before the upgrade. The latency curve reads utilization, and more capacity at the same load lowers it.
This assumes p99 falls in proportion to capacity. It follows 1 ÷ (1 − utilization) instead, which is why an upgrade from high on the curve buys more than its size ratio.
This is the p99 of an idle component, the floor no size gets below. At this load the new size still queues some requests, so p99 is above it.

explanation: Same load, 3 times the capacity: utilization falls from 80% to about 27%. The mean becomes 6 ÷ (1 − 0.267) ≈ 8.2 ms, and p99 is 4.61 times that. The gain is large because the component started high on the curve.

prompt: A component takes 32 ms to serve a request with nothing queued. However large a size you buy for it, what is the lowest p99 it can reach in this game’s model, to the nearest millisecond?

options.whyWrong: This is the mean with nothing queued, not the 99th percentile. Response times are still spread around it, and p99 sits about 4.6 times higher.
This is the median of an idle component. Half of all requests beat it; p99, the figure the SLO watches, is about 6.6 times higher.
More capacity only removes waiting. The work itself still takes its service time, so no size gets p99 anywhere near zero.

explanation: With no load nothing waits, so the mean response time is the service time itself, 32 ms. p99 is still the mean × ln 100 ≈ 4.61 × 32 ≈ 147 ms. Past that point more capacity buys nothing; only a shorter service time would.

prompt: At peak, 350/s arrive. Your app server serves 75/s and drops the rest, and the database behind it, which can serve 250/s, looks healthy. You upgrade the app server to 600/s. How many requests per second does the database drop now?

options.whyWrong: The database only looked healthy because the app server was dropping load in front of it. Once the app server serves everything, the database receives the full peak.
This is how much the old app server dropped. After the upgrade those requests reach the database, and its own capacity decides what it drops.
This is the room the database had while the app server was holding load back. That room is gone once the full peak arrives.

explanation: The new app server serves all 350/s, so every request it used to drop now reaches the database, one query each. The database serves 250/s and drops the other 100/s. It only looked healthy because the app server was dropping load before it arrived.

prompt: Your app server is already the largest size there is, which serves 500/s. Traffic averages 600/s and its busiest hour runs at 2.5 times that. How many requests per second does it drop at peak?

options.whyWrong: No size is unlimited. Past the largest size’s capacity the excess is dropped, and there is nothing bigger to upgrade to.
This measures the weekly mean against capacity. The week is resolved at its busiest hour, which is higher by the whole peak multiplier.
This is what the server completes, its full capacity. The question is what it turns away: the peak minus that.

explanation: Peak is 600 × 2.5 = 1,500/s against 500/s of capacity, so 1,000/s are dropped. There is no bigger size to buy: past the largest, serving more takes more than one server side by side.
